idw / Landesamt für Denkmalpflege und Archäologie Sachsen-Anhalt (8 Aug 2023) — publication of the excavation by Norma Henkel (about 150 circular enclosures known from the central and eastern European Middle Neolithic; Stroke-ornamented Pottery culture c. 4900–4600/4550 BC; found by Otto Braasch in 1991; open to the public since 2005; two concentric palisades; three entrances N, SE, SW; SE and SW gaps match winter-solstice sunrise and sunset; other gaps match the summer solstice and 30 April; cattle-skull fragments and about 30 horn cores in the ditch area; pits with burnt remains and human bones)

Volksstimme — 'Tausende Gäste am Ringheiligtum' (Goseck: 75 m diameter, three gates, double ring of oak palisades about 2 m high with an earth bank; about 25 km from the find site of the Nebra Sky Disc; part of the 'Himmelswege' tourist route)

abu_simbel.label: Wikipedia — Abu Simbel (Great Temple c. 1264–1244 BC, about 20 years' work; facade 33 m high and 38 m wide; four seated colossi about 20 m; frieze of 22 baboons; sanctuary statues of Ra-Horakhty, deified Ramesses, Amun-Ra and Ptah; sunlight on about 22 October and 22 February, Ptah 'a god connected with the realm of the dead' stays dark; birthday/coronation link 'allegedly', no direct evidence; date drift from precession plus relocation; Burckhardt 1813, Belzoni 1 August 1817; 1964–68 rescue: 1,036 blocks (807 Great Temple), raised 65 m and moved 208 m, US$41.7 million shared by Egypt and 48 countries, crowns and 19-tonne faces cut to fit 30-tonne cranes, sunbeam checked on 22 February 1966 at 63.1 m inside, inauguration 22 September 1968; UNESCO 1979)

Rosicrucian Egyptian Museum — New Kingdom Monuments: Abu Simbel (colossi about 21 m; light reaches the inner sanctuary on 22 October and 22 February and lights three seated statues; link with coronation and birth only hypothesised; moved 1964–68 about 64 m higher; because of the move and/or the slow drift of the Tropic of Cancer the events have shifted by about one day)

UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Nubian Monuments from Abu Simbel to Philae (inscribed 1979; temples of Ramesses II saved from the rising Nile by the international campaign launched by UNESCO; Great Temple carved out of an escarpment of solid rock, sunlight reaches the innermost chamber twice a year)
Wikipedia — Ramesses II (born c. 1303 BC, ruled c. 1279–1213 BC; accession most often dated to 31 May 1279 BC)
Serbian Wikipedia — Абу Симбел (spelling Abu Simbel, Ramzes II, Nefertari; temples raised 65 m higher; Burkhard found them in 1813)

angkor_wat.label: Wikipedia — Angkor Wat (built for Suryavarman II, ruled 1113–c. 1150, dedicated to Vishnu, gradually Buddhist from the late 13th century and still a Buddhist monastery; 162.6 ha, largest religious structure per Guinness; faces west — funerary reading by Glaize and Coedès, Vishnu link per Freeman and Jacques; Mount Meru quincunx; outer wall 1,024 × 802 m and 4.5 m high, moat 190 m wide, over 5 km round, 1.5 km E–W × 1.3 km N–S; central tower rises 43 m to 65 m above the ground; 5–10 million sandstone blocks up to 1.5 t from Mount Kulen ~40 km away; equinox sunrise over the central tower seen from the western causeway generally regarded as intentional; Mannikka's ideas met with interest and scepticism, 91 asuras/88 devas as days between solstice and equinox; never completely abandoned; António da Madalena 1586; Mouhot 1860; UNESCO 1992)
Stencel, Gifford & Morón (1976) — Astronomy and Cosmology at Angkor Wat, Science 193 (4250): 281–287, doi:10.1126/science.193.4250.281 (PubMed record)

Subhash Kak (arXiv, 1998) — The Solar Equation in Angkor Wat (summary of Stencel, Gifford and Morón: 1 hat = 0.435 m; rising Sun aligned with the western entrance on equinox and solstice days, 22 sighting lines; moat width 439.78 hat, west gate to end of causeway 867.03 hat, west gate to central tower 1,296.07 hat, bridge to centre 1,734.41 hat, read as the yugas of 432,000–1,728,000 years; upper level 189.00 + 176.37 = 365.37 hat)

Times Higher Education (2 Jan 1998) — Denise Heywood reviews Eleanor Mannikka's Angkor Wat: Time, Space and Kingship (University of Hawaii Press, 1996; measurements converted to Khmer cubits, recurring 54 and 108, the Sun rises exactly over the central tower on the spring equinox)
Guinness World Records — Largest religious structure (Angkor Wat, 162.6 ha, built for Vishnu by Suryavarman II in 1113–50)

nazca_lines.label: Wikipedia — Nazca lines (geoglyphs in the Nazca Desert of southern Peru between Nazca and Palpa, about 400 km south of Lima; made between 500 BC and AD 500, Paracas phase 400–200 BC and Nazca phase 200 BC–AD 500; made by removing reddish-brown iron-oxide-coated pebbles to expose yellow-grey subsoil; trenches 10–15 cm deep, more than half slightly over 33 cm wide, up to 1.8 m; combined length more than 1,300 km; best seen from about 500 m up but also from foothills; shapes usually one continuous line; more than 70 zoomorphic designs; largest figures nearly 370 m; hummingbird 93 m, condor 134 m, monkey 93 × 58 m, spider 47 m; Kosok 1940–41 and Reiche proposed astronomical markers; Hawkins and Aveni concluded the evidence was insufficient; Reiche's figures-as-constellations idea and Pitluga's spider-as-Orion claim criticised by Aveni for ignoring the figure's other 12 lines; Reinhard's water-worship interpretation; von Däniken's 1968 landing-site claim called pseudoscientific, Nickell reproduced figures with period tools; Yamagata University fieldwork since 2006, 143 new geoglyphs with IBM Japan in 2019, 303 found with AI in 2024; 25 Paracas geoglyphs found by drone in Palpa in 2018; UNESCO 1994)

National Geographic — 'Why the Nasca lines are among Peru's greatest mysteries' (over 800 straight lines, 300 geometric figures and 70 animal and plant designs; biomorphs 50–1,200 ft long; lines made by removing rust-coloured surface rocks to expose light ground; Kosok at the foot of a line on 22 June 1941, a day after the winter solstice, saw the sunset aligned with it and called the pampa 'the largest astronomy book in the world'; Maria Reiche studied the lines for 40 years and argued for an astronomical calendar; the Kosok–Reiche theory questioned from the 1970s; Reinhard: lines led to places of rituals for water and fertility; Aveni: straight lines and trapezoids related to water and used in rituals; most lines made by the Nasca people)

EBSCO Research Starters — Nasca Lines (lines made by removing a thin layer of dark rock to reveal lighter soil; Reiche surveyed more than 250 lines; in 1968 Gerald Hawkins used his Stonehenge computer program to check 186 lines against the Sun, Moon, planets and stars: 39 matched major Sun and Moon directions but half could be accounted for by pure chance, so the astronomical hypothesis could not account for most of the lines; von Däniken's Chariots of the Gods, 1968)

Aveni, A. F. (2000), 'Solving the Mystery of the Nasca Lines', Archaeology 53(3) (three decades of fieldwork on the pampa; the lines were made to walk upon — they were pathways; ritual on the ray centres and trapezoids connected with the ritual acquisition of water; possible link between sunrise/sunset positions and the arrival of water in the valleys; not the product of a single superhuman effort)

Sakai et al. (2024), PNAS 121(40):e2407652121 — 'AI-accelerated Nazca survey nearly doubles the number of known figurative geoglyphs and sheds light on their purpose' (Yamagata University with IBM Research; 430 figurative geoglyphs known after nearly a century, 303 new ones confirmed in six months of field survey, September 2022–February 2023; line-type figures average 90 m and mostly show wild animals, placed by the network of lines and trapezoids and probably used for community rituals; relief-type figures average 9 m, mostly people, domesticated animals and decapitated heads, an average 43 m from walking trails; line-type figures probably made in the Nasca period, 100 BC–AD 650)
Serbian Wikipedia — Наска линије (spelling Naska linije, Naska, Palpa, Lima; geoglyphs of people, monkeys, birds and whales, from ten to several hundred metres; UNESCO 1994)

gobekli_tepe.label: Wikipedia — Göbekli Tepe ('Potbelly Hill'; Pre-Pottery Neolithic, inhabited from about 9500 to at least 8000 BC, earliest structures 9500–9000 BC (late PPNA), later phases PPNB; 15 m high, 8 ha tell covered with domestic structures, quarries and rock-cut cisterns holding at least 150 m³; 2019 findings of houses, cereal processing (over 7,000 grinding stones) and a water supply revise the 'sanctuary for nomads' reading; enclosures 10–30 m across, four excavated, geophysics shows 16 more, nearly 200 pillars; slabs quarried about 100 m away with flint tools; enclosures damaged by landslides and rebuilt over eight phases spanning at least 1,500 years; noted in a 1963 survey (Çambel, Braidwood; Peter Benedict took pillar tops for grave markers); Klaus Schmidt recognised it in October 1994 and dug from 1995 until his death in 2014; now Istanbul University, Şanlıurfa Museum and DAI under Necmi Karul; about 10% excavated; Pillar 43 in Enclosure D, the 'Vulture Stone'; astronomical-observatory claims largely rejected by the team; Karahan Tepe and other Taş Tepeler sites; UNESCO World Heritage 2018)

Wikipedia (German) — Göbekli Tepe (tell about 15 m high and about 300 m across at the base; enclosures 10–30 m across; Enclosure D oval, maximum inner diameter 20 m, best preserved and most richly decorated, central Pillars 18 and 31 over 5 m tall and at least a metre taller than the ring pillars; Enclosure C over 30 m overall with up to four concentric walls; three unfinished T-pillars still in the bedrock, the largest over 7 m long, more than 3 m wide at the head, estimated at about 50 tonnes; Schmidt recognised pillar fragments in October 1994; Sweatman and Tsikritsis 2017: Pillar 43 ('Geierstein') as a date near the summer solstice of 10,950 BC ± 250 linked to the Younger Dryas impact, fox and boar as the Taurid meteor showers, later a 'solar calendar' reading — disputed; Graham Hancock's lost Ice Age culture 'without empirical basis'; UNESCO World Heritage 1 July 2018)

Tepe Telegrams (Göbekli Tepe Research Project, German Archaeological Institute) — FAQ (mound about 300 m across, up to 15 m high, about 9 ha, entirely man-made; excavations every year since 1995 under Klaus Schmidt, after 2014 Lee Clare, from 2020 directed by Necmi Karul, who also leads Karahan Tepe, both part of the Taş Tepeler project; central pair of pillars more than 5 m tall; special buildings A–D partly excavated, E, F, G and H found later; PPN A about 9600–8800 BC and early/middle PPN B about 8800–8000 BC; fire installations, food remains, cisterns and burials show people lived there — now a settlement with a pronounced ritual component; roofs conceivable; no link found so far between astronomical phenomena and the orientation of pillars or buildings; 'temple' not the best term; no connection with Stonehenge or the Garden of Eden)

Tepe Telegrams — 'More than a vulture: A response to Sweatman and Tsikritsis' (Jens Notroff, 3 July 2017; reply by J. Notroff, O. Dietrich, L. Clare et al. in Mediterranean Archaeology and Archaeometry 17(2), 2017, 57–63: many pillars not in their original positions and reused, buildings probably roofed, which limits use as sky observatories; the proposed date for Pillar 43, 10,950 BC ± 250, is 700–1,000 years older than the oldest radiocarbon date for Enclosure D; asterisms are not stable across times and cultures; picking a few pillars out of more than 60 is arbitrary; the headless man's phallus contradicts a reading of death and catastrophe; the Younger Dryas impact hypothesis is itself disputed)

Serbian Wikipedia — Гобекли Тепе (spelling Gobekli Tepe, Klaus Šmit, Nevali Čori; monumental Neolithic site in south-eastern Anatolia, about 9600–8200 BC; Šmit's research from 1994; T-shaped limestone pillars in rings with two taller pillars in the middle; UNESCO World Heritage; still gives the older 'temple without a settlement' view)

oumuamua.label: Meech et al. (2017), Nature 552:378 — 'A brief visit from a red and extremely elongated interstellar asteroid' (discovery paper: found by Pan-STARRS1 on 19 October 2017; hyperbolic orbit; brightness varies about tenfold, implying an axis ratio of at least 10:1; reddish surface like outer-Solar-System bodies; no dust coma detected)

ESO press release eso1737 (20 November 2017) — 'ESO Observations Show First Interstellar Asteroid is Like Nothing Seen Before' (brightness varies by a factor of ten every 7.3 hours; about ten times as long as wide; dark red colour; completely inert, no dust; estimated at least 400 m long; came from the direction of Vega, which was not there 300,000 years ago; Hawaiian name, 1I designation)

NASA Science — 'Oumuamua (discovered 19 October 2017; up to 400 m long and perhaps 10 times as long as wide; reddish; perihelion on 9 September 2017 at 87.3 km/s; about 26.4 km/s incoming speed; first classed as a comet, then an asteroid, then found to be accelerating slightly like a comet; name means 'a messenger from afar arriving first')

Micheli et al. (2018), Nature 559:223 — 'Non-gravitational acceleration in the trajectory of 1I/2017 U1 (ʻOumuamua)' (acceleration detected at 30 sigma, radial and falling off roughly as 1/r²; consistent with comet-like outgassing although no activity was seen; tumbling rotation, cometary-like surface)

Bergner & Seligman (2023), Nature 615:610 — 'Acceleration of 1I/ʻOumuamua from radiolytically produced H₂ in H₂O ice' (cosmic rays turn water ice into trapped molecular hydrogen during the interstellar journey; warming near the Sun releases it, which can explain the push without a visible coma)
ʻOumuamua ISSI Team (2019), Nature Astronomy 3:594 — 'The natural history of ʻOumuamua' (review: in all cases the observations are consistent with a purely natural origin)

Bialy & Loeb (2018), ApJ Letters 868:L1 — 'Could Solar Radiation Pressure Explain ʻOumuamua's Peculiar Acceleration?' (the light-sail proposal: would need a sheet about 0.3–0.9 mm thick; raises an artificial probe as an 'exotic' possibility)

Wikipedia — 1I/ʻOumuamua (discovered by Robert Weryk with Pan-STARRS1, Haleakalā; eccentricity 1.20; 26.33 km/s interstellar speed; perihelion 0.255 AU; observed for 80 days; tumbling; size estimates from 100 m to 1,000 m long, or a 115 × 111 × 19 m disc (Mashchenko 2019); Allen Telescope Array and Breakthrough Listen found no radio signals; hydrogen-ice, nitrogen-ice and H₂-from-water-ice explanations)

atlas_3i.label: Wikipedia — 3I/ATLAS (C/2025 N1; discovered 1 July 2025 by ATLAS at Río Hurtado, Chile; third interstellar object after 1I/ʻOumuamua and 2I/Borisov; hyperbolic excess speed ~58 km/s vs 26 km/s for ʻOumuamua and 32 km/s for Borisov; perihelion 29 October 2025 at 1.356 AU; passed Mars 3 October 2025, Earth at 1.80 AU on 19 December 2025, Jupiter at 0.358 AU on 16 March 2026; age estimates 7.6–14 Gyr (Hopkins et al.) and 3–11 Gyr (Taylor & Seligman); JWST CO2-dominated coma; Ni detected, Fe initially not; Loeb's alien-technology paper and the criticism by Lintott, Lawler, Seligman and others; observed by ExoMars TGO, Psyche and Juice)

NASA — Comet 3I/ATLAS (discovered 1 July 2025 by the NASA-funded ATLAS telescope in Río Hurtado, Chile; pre-discovery images back to 14 June 2025; nucleus upper limit 5.6 km, possibly as small as 440 m (Aug 2025); perihelion around 30 October 2025 at ~1.4 AU, just inside Mars' orbit; closest to Earth ~1.8 AU (~270 million km), no threat; observed by Hubble, Webb, TESS, Swift, SPHEREx, Perseverance, MRO, MAVEN, Europa Clipper, Lucy, Psyche, Parker Solar Probe, PUNCH and SOHO)

ESA — Comet 3I/ATLAS frequently asked questions (about 250,000 km/h at perihelion; size from a few hundred metres to a few kilometres; billions of years old; perihelion 203 million km on 29 October 2025; ~29 million km from Mars on 3 October 2025; closest to Earth ~270 million km on 19 December 2025; observed by ExoMars TGO, Mars Express, Juice and SOHO)

Hui, Jewitt, Mutchler et al. (2026, ApJ Letters) — Nucleus and Postperihelion Activity of Interstellar Object 3I/ATLAS Observed by Hubble Space Telescope (first detection of the nucleus in HST images of December 2025–January 2026: effective radius 1.3 ± 0.2 km assuming a comet-like albedo of 0.04; agrees with the estimate from its non-gravitational acceleration)

Cordiner et al. (2025) — JWST detection of a carbon dioxide dominated gas coma surrounding interstellar object 3I/ATLAS (NIRSpec at 3.32 AU; CO2/H2O ratio 7.6 ± 0.3, among the highest ever seen in a comet; H2O, CO, OCS, water ice and dust also present)

Hutsemékers, Manfroid, Jehin & Opitom (2026, A&A) — Pre-perihelion evolution of the NiI/FeI abundance ratio in the coma of 3I/ATLAS: from extreme to normal (VLT: nickel at all epochs, iron only inside 2.64 AU; the ratio fell to normal comet values; explained by sublimation of nickel and iron carbonyls)

Hibberd, Crowl & Loeb (2025, arXiv preprint) — Is the Interstellar Object 3I/ATLAS Alien Technology? (the speculation itself, described by the authors as 'largely a pedagogical exercise')

borisov.label: Jewitt et al. Jewitt et al. (2020), ApJ Letters 896:L39 — 'Outburst and Splitting of Interstellar Comet 2I/Borisov' (arXiv preprint; March 2020 outburst outbound at 2.8 AU ejected about 2 × 10⁷ kg of dust, about 1/10,000 of the nucleus mass; short-lived 'double nucleus' on 30 March 2020, explained by metre-sized boulders breaking up; the comet survives largely unscathed)

NASA Science — Comet 2I/Borisov (first confirmed interstellar comet, found by Crimean amateur Gennady Borisov on 30 August 2019; Hubble images in October and December 2019, nucleus too small to be seen; about 177,000 km/h; fragment broke off in March 2020; estimated up to about 975 m across)

Wikipedia — 2I/Borisov (discovered with a self-built 0.65 m telescope at MARGO, Nauchnij, Crimea; eccentricity 3.36; 32 km/s hyperbolic excess speed; perihelion 2.0 AU on 8 December 2019; closest to Earth 28 December 2019; tail about 14 times the size of Earth (Yale, November 2019); CO-rich, water- and C₂-poor; nucleus upper limits 0.4–0.5 km)

planet_nine.label: Wikipedia — Planet Nine (hypothetical; Trujillo & Sheppard 2014 noticed clustered orbits; Batygin & Brown 2016: ~10 Earth masses, chance alignment 0.007%; early estimates 5–10 Earth masses, 2–4 Earth radii, 400–800 AU, 10,000–20,000-year orbit; Siraj et al. 2025 fit 4.4 ± 1.1 Earth masses at 290 ± 30 AU; Shankman et al. 2017 (OSSOS), Bernardinelli et al. 2020 and Napier et al. 2021 found no clustering after correcting for bias; alternatives: self-gravitating disc (Madigan & McCourt 2016, Sefilian & Touma 2019), primordial black hole (Scholtz & Unwin 2019); WISE and Pan-STARRS found nothing; 2017 OF201 and 2023 KQ14 orbits misaligned)

Caltech news (20 January 2016) — Caltech Researchers Find Evidence of a Real Ninth Planet (about 10 Earth masses, ~20 times Neptune's average distance, 10,000–20,000-year orbit; six distant Kuiper Belt objects point the same way; 0.007% chance; Sedna; both researchers started out sceptical; Brown and Pluto's demotion)

NASA — Hypothetical Planet X (Batygin and Brown, January 2016, did not observe a planet; 5–10 Earth masses, 20–30 times farther than Neptune on average, 10,000–20,000 years per orbit; 'remains theoretical'; debate over whether it exists; Percival Lowell's 1915 Planet X)

Batygin & Brown (2016, Astronomical Journal 151:22) — Evidence for a Distant Giant Planet in the Solar System (perihelia and orbital planes of distant Kuiper Belt objects tightly confined, 0.007% chance; explained by a distant eccentric planet of more than ~10 Earth masses)

Shankman et al. (2017) — OSSOS VI. Striking biases in the detection of large semimajor axis trans-Neptunian objects (OSSOS's eight distant objects are consistent with a uniform, unclustered distribution once survey bias is modelled)

Napier et al. (2021, Planetary Science Journal) — No Evidence for Orbital Clustering in the Extreme Trans-Neptunian Objects (14 objects from DES, OSSOS and Sheppard & Trujillo; consistent with a uniform population at the 17–94% level)

Siraj, Chyba & Tremaine (2025, ApJ 978) — Orbit of a Possible Planet X (clustering at ~3σ in longitude of perihelion for objects beyond 170 AU; best fit 4.4 ± 1.1 Earth masses, 290 ± 30 AU, inclination ~7°)

Siraj, Chyba & Tremaine (2025, MNRAS) — Measuring the Mean Plane of the Distant Kuiper Belt (a warp at 80–400 AU at 98% confidence; most likely cause an unseen planet between Mercury and Earth in mass at roughly 100–200 AU — 'Planet Y'; LSST should confirm or refute it)

Cheng, Li & Yang (2025) — Discovery of a dwarf planet candidate in an extremely wide orbit: 2017 OF201 (about 700 km, semi-major axis 830 AU; its longitude of perihelion lies outside the clustering attributed to Planet Nine)

Serbian Wikipedia — Планета девет (spelling Planeta devet; Konstantin Batigin, Majkl Braun; ekstremni transneptunski objekti; 5–10 Zemljinih masa; 400–800 AJ, later 290 ± 30 AJ; 2017 OF201 and 2023 KQ14 challenge the hypothesis)

muon.label: Wikipedia — Muon (mass 105.66 MeV/c², about 206.77 electron masses; mean lifetime 2.1969811 µs; discovered by Anderson and Neddermeyer at Caltech in 1936 in cosmic rays, confirmed by Street and Stevenson in 1937; Rabi's 'Who ordered that?'; about 10,000 muons per square metre per minute at sea level; time dilation lets them reach the ground; muonic hydrogen; muon-catalysed fusion; muon tomography from Alvarez's Khafre search to the 2017 void in Khufu's pyramid)

Particle Data Group (2022) — Review of cosmic rays, §30.3 Muons at the surface (most muons are produced typically 15 km up and lose about 2 GeV before reaching the ground; mean energy at the ground about 4 GeV; integral vertical intensity about 70 m⁻² s⁻¹ sr⁻¹, i.e. about 1 cm⁻² min⁻¹ for horizontal detectors)

Wikipedia — Experimental testing of time dilation (Rossi–Hall: Echo Lake 3,240 m vs Denver 1,616 m, muons above 0.99c; Frisch–Smith 1962 film / 1963 paper: about 563 muons per hour on Mount Washington (1,917 m), about 412 per hour at sea level in Cambridge against about 27 expected without time dilation, dilation factor 8.8 ± 0.8; Bailey et al. 1977 CERN muon storage ring)

Morishima et al. (2017, Nature) — Discovery of a big void in Khufu's Pyramid by observation of cosmic-ray muons (void above the Grand Gallery with a similar cross-section and at least 30 m long; seen with nuclear emulsion films (Nagoya), scintillator hodoscopes (KEK) and gas detectors (CEA))

Fermilab (3 June 2025) — Muon g-2 announces most precise measurement of the magnetic anomaly of the muon (final value 0.001 165 920 705, precision 127 parts per billion; data 2018–2023; the Theory Initiative's new prediction lies close to it, the gap between data-driven and lattice methods remains unresolved; ring moved from Brookhaven in 2013; J-PARC follow-up in the 2030s)

CERN — Muon collider (muons are about 200 times heavier than electrons and emit about two billion times less synchrotron radiation; a 10 TeV muon collider could rival a 100 TeV proton collider; the 2.2 µs lifetime is the main technical hurdle; International Muon Collider Collaboration design study)

Wikipedia — Muon-catalyzed fusion (predicted by Frank and Sakharov; observed by Alvarez's team in a Berkeley hydrogen bubble chamber in 1956; the muon pulls the nuclei about 200 times closer than in an ordinary molecule; best result about 150 d–t fusions per muon at Los Alamos, short of break-even)

superconductivity.label: Wikipedia — Superconductivity (Kamerlingh Onnes, 8 April 1911: mercury's resistance vanished at 4.2 K; persistent currents with an experimental lifetime of at least 100,000 years, a superconducting gravimeter coil current in Belgium kept from 4 August 1995 to 31 March 2024; Meissner and Ochsenfeld 1933; BCS theory 1957, Nobel 1972; Bednorz and Müller's cuprates 1986, Nobel 1987; YBCO about 92–93 K above liquid nitrogen's 77 K; mercury cuprates above 130 K; MgB₂ 39 K; MRI magnets and SQUIDs)
NobelPrize.org — Physics 1987: J. Georg Bednorz and K. Alexander Müller 'for their important break-through in the discovery of superconductivity in ceramic materials'

Drozdov, Eremets et al. (2019, Nature) — Superconductivity at 250 K in lanthanum hydride under high pressures (LaH₁₀, about 170 GPa; zero resistance, isotope effect and the drop of Tc in a magnetic field)

Deng, Chu et al. (2026, PNAS) — Ambient-pressure 151-K superconductivity in HgBa₂Ca₂Cu₃O₈₊δ via pressure quench (Hg-1223: about 133 K as made, 164 K under pressure; 139–151 K kept at ambient pressure after pressure quenching; the ambient-pressure record had been unchanged since 1993)

Nature news (7 November 2023) — Nature retracts controversial superconductivity paper by embattled physicist (Ranga Dias's March 2023 claim of near-room-temperature superconductivity in nitrogen-doped lutetium hydride; his 2020 carbonaceous sulfur hydride paper had been retracted in 2022)

Nature news (16 August 2023) — LK-99 isn't a superconductor: how science sleuths solved the mystery (copper sulfide impurities explain the resistance drop near 104 °C and the partial levitation; pure crystals are insulators)
CERN — Pulling together: superconducting electromagnets (1,232 main dipoles, each 15 m long, 8.3 tesla, 11,080 amperes)
Wikipedia (sr) — Superprovodnost (Serbian term: superprovodnost, superprovodnik; Majsnerov efekat, Kuperovi parovi)

quantum_computing.label: Wikipedia — Quantum computing (qubits in superposition and entanglement; algorithms rely on interference, a measurement gives one outcome; Feynman's 1981 proposal and Deutsch's 1985 universal quantum computer; Shor's algorithm 1994 and Grover's quadratic speed-up; platforms: superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photons; decoherence and the need for error correction; no exponential speed-up known for most everyday problems)

Arute et al. (2019), Nature 574:505 — 'Quantum supremacy using a programmable superconducting processor' (Sycamore, 53 working qubits; random circuit sampling in about 200 seconds)

Google Quantum AI (2025), Nature 638:920 — 'Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold' (Willow, 105 qubits; surface-code logical qubits of distance 3, 5 and 7; logical error rate roughly halves with each step up; the distance-7 logical qubit outlives its best physical qubit) — with Google's Willow announcement of 9 December 2024 (random circuit sampling in under 5 minutes versus an estimated 10²⁵ years on the Frontier supercomputer; qubit lifetimes near 100 µs)

Google Research blog (22 October 2025) — 'A verifiable quantum advantage' (Quantum Echoes / out-of-time-order correlator on 65 of Willow's 105 qubits, published in Nature; Google estimates each data point would take about 3.2 years on Frontier, about 13,000 times longer; result can be checked by another quantum computer of similar quality; separate proof-of-principle molecule experiment matched NMR)

Gidney (May 2025), arXiv:2505.15917 — 'How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits' (under a week of run time; assumes 0.1% gate error, 1 µs surface-code cycle; 20 times fewer qubits than the 2019 estimate of 20 million)

Gutmann & Neuhaus (2025), IACR ePrint 2025/1237 — 'Replication of Quantum Factorisation Records with an 8-bit Home Computer, an Abacus, and a Dog' (published quantum factoring records such as 15 and 21 rely on preprocessing that already uses the answer; matched with a 1981 VIC-20, an abacus and a dog)

NIST (13 August 2024) — 'NIST Releases First 3 Finalized Post-Quantum Encryption Standards' (FIPS 203 ML-KEM, FIPS 204 ML-DSA, FIPS 205 SLH-DSA; designed to resist attacks by future quantum computers; organisations urged to start migrating now)
